evidence_set: Clinical review for clinicians by four clinical pharmacists (schools of pharmacy in Kansas, Arkansas and California). PubMed and Google Scholar were searched for English-language literature from 1946 to 2016 with the keywords urine drug test, screen, false-positive, false-negative and abuse and individual drug names, with references cited in retrieved papers added; only publications on urine testing in humans or human samples were kept; the numbers of records and the selection steps are not reported, and no method for appraising the cited studies is described (the text comments on the evidence for some agents only).

Table 2, 'Approximate Drug Detection Time in the Urine', adapted from the authors' 2008 review, gives one value per row with no cutoff, test or amount (only marijuana and synthetic cannabinoids are split by pattern of use): alcohol 7–12 hours; amphetamine 48 hours; methamphetamine 48 hours; barbiturates, short-acting (pentobarbital) 24 hours, long-acting (phenobarbital) 3 weeks; benzodiazepines, short-acting (lorazepam) 3 days, long-acting (diazepam) 30 days; cocaine metabolites 2–4 days; marijuana, single use 3 days, moderate use (4 times a week) 5–7 days, chronic use (daily) 10–15 days, chronic heavy smoker more than 30 days; codeine 48 hours; heroin (morphine) 48 hours; hydromorphone 2–4 days; methadone 3 days; morphine 48–72 hours; oxycodone 2–4 days; phencyclidine 8 days; synthetic cannabinoids, single use 72 hours, chronic use more than 72 hours; synthetic cathinones variable. Its nine sources (references 9–17) are a 1987 report of a Council on Scientific Affairs in JAMA, a 2004 review of urine testing in pain medicine, a textbook on psychoactive drugs, the authors' 2008 review, two laboratory web pages answering questions on synthetic cannabinoid testing, a psychiatry textbook chapter, Verstraete (2004) and a 2005 article in a pharmacists' newsletter. The text calls these standard detection times and says detection depends on half-life, metabolites, interactions, dosing interval, amount, chronic or occasional use, time of last use, body mass, urine pH and concentration, and kidney or liver impairment.

Screening immunoassays for cannabis react to several THC metabolites (federal cutoff 50 ng/mL; some laboratories may use a lower cutoff of 20 ng/mL); confirmation by GC-MS or LC-MS/MS is specific for THCCOOH, with a federal cutoff of 15 ng/mL. Detection depends on route, amount and potency, frequency of use, body mass and metabolic rate; chronic use leads to THC accumulating in fat and slow elimination, so cannabis can be detected in urine for more than 30 days after stopping in people who used chronically, whereas a single exposure in people who do not use it is typically detectable for up to 72 hours.

evidence_set: Clinical review for clinicians by four clinical pharmacists. PubMed and Google Scholar were searched for English-language literature from 1946 to 2016 with the keywords urine drug test, screen, false-positive, false-negative and abuse and individual drug names, plus references cited in retrieved papers; only publications on urine testing in humans or human samples were kept; the numbers of records and the selection steps are not reported, and no method for appraising the cited studies is described (the text comments on the evidence for some agents only). The introduction says that misreading a result (false positive or false negative) can have significant consequences, such as loss of a job or incarceration.

Amphetamine immunoassays are the screens most commonly associated with false positives, which the authors attribute to other cross-reacting drugs and substances, adding that antibodies specific to amphetamine and methamphetamine are hard to develop because of their structures; the assays detect amphetamine, dextroamphetamine, methamphetamine, MDA, MDEA and MDMA. Agents commonly linked to false-positive amphetamine results are pseudoephedrine and ephedrine, bupropion, labetalol and ranitidine; metformin has also been linked; selegiline is metabolized to l-methamphetamine and l-amphetamine; lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) is converted to d-amphetamine and will be detected; in a Department of Defense analysis, the supplement ingredient DMAA was found in 92.3% of the false-positive amphetamine samples that GC-MS then confirmed negative.

Medicines reported to cross-react with cannabis immunoassays include proton pump inhibitors (evidence limited to one pantoprazole case report and its package insert), NSAIDs (in Rollins et al., 2 of 510 samples gave false positives for cannabis, one from a patient taking ibuprofen daily and one from a patient taking naproxen long term; interference appears rare) and efavirenz (well documented; attributed to its glucuronide metabolite). Several baby wash products, investigated because false-positive THC screens in newborns had increased, gave dose-dependent responses on THC immunoassays, many positive at a 20 ng/mL cutoff and none reaching the standard 50 ng/mL.

True positives from medicines: dronabinol, a synthetic THC, tests positive for THC and cannot be told apart from plant THC by confirmatory tests, whereas nabilone tests negative (p. 7); codeine is metabolized to morphine and norcodeine, all three detectable in urine after codeine, and codeine and hydrocodone metabolism can produce small amounts of hydrocodone and hydromorphone respectively, which should not be read as use of those drugs when high concentrations of codeine or (as printed) hydromorphone are detected (p. 10); lisdexamfetamine is converted to d-amphetamine and is detected (p. 13).
Cannabinoids, 7th paragraph (p. 7); Central Nervous System Depressants › Opioids, 7th paragraph (p. 10); CNS Stimulants › Amphetamines, 3rd paragraph (p. 13)
Central Nervous System Depressants › Opioids, 4th paragraph (p. 9, continuing p. 10), 5th and 10th paragraphs (p. 10)

Coca leaves used in teas, drinks and other products in some countries can make cocaine screens positive. Cocaine screens test for benzoylecgonine and show minimal cross-reactivity; the claim, repeated by internet sources and review articles, that amoxicillin causes false positives lacks evidence, and Reisfield et al. found no false-positive results for cocaine metabolites with amoxicillin on 4 immunoassays; cocaine used as a topical anaesthetic in ear, nose and throat or eye procedures can give true positives, while benzocaine, lidocaine, procaine and tetracaine, being structurally distinct, do not produce false positives.

Incidental exposure to alcohol through hand sanitizers or mouthwash can produce positive urine test results; in the same paragraph the metabolite ethyl glucuronide is the preferred test because it can be detected in urine for 2 to 5 days after drinking, and a ratio of ethyl glucuronide to ethyl sulfate may help tell drinking from incidental exposure.

evidence_set: Systematic review of studies done in Iran, searched to June 2019 in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and the Persian SID, with expert contacts, unpublished data and reference lists; proportions pooled with random-effects models (Freeman–Tukey transformation); not preregistered, and the authors call the results exploratory. 84 studies, 62 on tramadol-related poisoning, seizures or deaths; no study gave the frequency of poisoning or death among people who use tramadol. Of the 55 studies of tramadol poisoning and its consequences (Tables 3–6; the seven forensic death studies are counted separately), the text says none met all quality items and three met fewer than five, and only one was national, the others from 17 of 31 provinces.

The authors write, citing other work, that tramadol relieves pain mainly through its breakdown product O-desmethyltramadol, made by the liver enzyme CYP2D6, whose activity varies with other medicines and with genes (poor, intermediate and ultra-rapid metabolizers), and suggest, citing one Iranian study, that a high share of ultra-rapid metabolizers may partly explain Iran's high rates of poisoning, seizures and deaths; the review reports no metabolizer data from its included studies. They summarize seizures as almost 35% and deaths as 0.7% of admitted tramadol poisonings. Stated limitations include no longitudinal study of health outcomes in people using tramadol and, in some toxicological and forensic studies, no definite confirmation that tramadol was the only or main substance.

evidence_set: Study 2: 12 people (6 men, 6 women; mean age 28.6 ± 1.9 years, range 21 to 40); women tested in the follicular phase; two people (one man, one woman) vomited within 15 minutes of finishing the water in their MDMA sessions, and those data were excluded. No significant effect of MDMA was detected on maximum ADH (F(1,15) = 0.113, p = 0.74) or on maximum copeptin (F(1,9) = 0.019, p = 0.89); 14 of 120 ADH samples (8 from placebo sessions) were not analysable because of temperature-control failures, and 1 of 72 copeptin samples was missing.

Urine was collected, pooled before dosing and over 0-8 and 8-24 hours, but no urine result of any kind is reported; the limitations paragraph says that urine osmolality, which could have greatly aided interpretation, was not measured, that thirst was not measured, and that both studies used a single dose. No significant relationship was detected between ADH and the fall in sodium, and peak MDMA or HMMA concentrations did not appear to predict it significantly once condition was in the model. The authors state that they did not establish a mechanism and found no relationship between the lowered sodium and ADH or copeptin (although Results 3.8 report that copeptin significantly predicted serum sodium at 2 and 3 hours in Study 2, F(1,32) = 4.22, p = 0.048, apparently independent of condition), and suggest that the water load may have suppressed the hormone in Study 2 or that their ADH assay was too variable.

Double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study (random order, by the abstract) in 32 healthy volunteers (16 men, 16 women; aged 20 to 31; 22 had never taken MDMA and 10 had taken it fewer than five times), each given MDMA 125 mg and placebo at least 10 days apart. Plasma copeptin, the C-terminal part of the vasopressin precursor, was measured before and 1 and 2 hours after the dose: the authors report that MDMA did not alter it (no test statistic printed; Figure 4B shows mean changes from baseline), while oxytocin, cortisol and prolactin rose. No sodium measurement, and no urine measure other than drug screening before sessions, is reported.

evidence_set: The authors state that DIMS results are not, by definition, an exact representation of the Dutch ecstasy market, since they depend on samples people hand in, and call DIMS a qualitative monitor of contents. Compared with tablets seized from people going out (85% of which were recognised immediately with the DIMS database), DIMS tablets over-represent low- and high-MDMA tablets and tablets with other active substances, which the authors suggest may be explained by people preferring to submit tablets whose effects differed from what they expected. All six authors work in the DIMS programme at the Trimbos Institute; DIMS is financed by the Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.

evidence_set: The letter, by Bonnet and Scherbaum (authors of a 2017 systematic review of how addictive gabapentinoids are) and a pain specialist, comments on Evoy et al.'s systematic review update. It accepts the limits that review itself states (small samples, mostly retrospective designs, homogeneous groups of people dependent on opioids and other substances) and says clinical studies of people without past or present substance use disorders are lacking; argues that the reported outcomes are often surrogate and relatively rare and that the authors know of only a minuscule number of people worldwide seeking treatment for gabapentinoid misuse; says they know of no study that accounted for predictors and confounders well enough to support a causal link between gabapentinoid use or misuse and harms including psychological dependence and death (a PubMed search for mediation analyses found no human studies), and that among the review's 46 new observational studies only very few prospective investigations addressed gabapentinoid addiction and deaths, and those were small, less specific or limited to people using opioids; and calls for well-powered, controlled prospective studies.

The letter proposes that gabapentinoids might protect people who use opioids by replacing riskier drugs, adding that this has not been investigated (6th paragraph); it acknowledges that they may raise the risk of adverse outcomes in people using other substances through synergistic depression of the nervous system and perhaps of breathing, and says that 'the latter' has not been proven mechanistically or clinically (8th paragraph). Declarations: the authors had written two reviews on the subject, and one author received honoraria from several pharmaceutical companies and took part in industry-funded clinical trials in the last 3 years.
